title: SLDS, accessibility, responsive behavior, and mobile considerations
objectives: Prefer Lightning base components and SLDS blueprints over unstyled HTML for accessibility and look-and-feel.
Explain shadow DOM CSS scoping, :host, and why a parent cannot style a child's internals.
Use styling hooks instead of hard-coded colors so themes and density still work.
Call out keyboard, focus, and Salesforce mobile constraints rather than desktop-only layouts.
diagnostic_question: A custom LWC looks fine on a wide monitor but fails a keyboard audit, overflows on a phone, and ignores the org's brand colors. What do you inspect first: SLDS, accessibility, responsive behavior, or mobile considerations?
definition: SLDS, accessibility, responsive behavior, and mobile considerations are how an LWC looks, can be used with assistive technology, reflows across widths, and behaves in the Salesforce mobile app. The Lightning Web Components Developer Guide tells you to follow WCAG, prefer base components with built-in Lightning Design System styling and accessibility, or build from an SLDS blueprint. Component CSS is scoped in shadow DOM; parents style a child as a single host element, not its internals. ([Component Accessibility](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-components-accessibility.html); [CSS Stylesheets](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-components-css.html))
why_it_matters: Interviewers fail 'it looks like Salesforce' answers that ignore keyboard focus, contrast, and mobile. Hard-coded px and hex also break SLDS themes. Shadow DOM surprises candidates who try to reach into a child with a descendant selector from the parent.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a touring concert hall. SLDS is the house instrument spec so every night sounds like the same orchestra. Accessibility is ramps, hearing loops, and large-print programs so every guest can take part. Responsive behavior is reseating when the hall shrinks. Mobile is the van show: fewer seats, bigger tap targets, no assumption there is a mouse. You do not invent a new violin shape for one song when the house already has a standard.
deeper_explanation: To create accessible components, use accessibility attributes and handle focus. Follow WCAG. Prefer a Lightning base component for built-in SLDS styling and accessibility. If none fits, use an SLDS blueprint. ([Component Accessibility](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-components-accessibility.html))

A component stylesheet is automatically applied when it shares the component name. Shadow DOM scopes those rules so they do not leak out or get overwritten by the page. A parent can style a child as one element (for example a border on c-child) but cannot reach into the child's h1. The child styles its host with :host. ID selectors are not supported as authored because IDs are transformed at runtime. Use styling hooks for colors and sizes instead of one-off hex values. ([CSS Stylesheets](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-components-css.html))

Responsive behavior in Lightning uses SLDS grid, size classes, and layout that reflows. Do not assume a 1200px record page. Hide nonessential columns before they overflow. lightning-datatable and dense pages have extra cost on small viewports (LWC-011).

Mobile considerations: the Salesforce mobile app is a supported LWC target, but navigation and some modules differ from desktop (LWC-008). Follow accessible mobile design guidelines referenced from the accessibility topic. Large tap targets, avoid hover-only actions, and test on a phone form factor. Do not invent a second data model 'for mobile' when the same LWC can reflow.

mental_model.analogy: A touring concert hall: house instrument spec (SLDS), ramps and hearing loops (accessibility), reseating a smaller hall (responsive), van show (mobile).
useful_mapping: house instrument spec → SLDS / base components / blueprints
ramps and hearing loops → WCAG, labels, focus, contrast
reseating a smaller hall → responsive grid and hidden columns
van show → Salesforce mobile: tap targets, no hover
each musician's mute → shadow DOM scoped CSS
conductor cannot retune a player's internal pegs from the podium → parent cannot style child internals
where_it_breaks: A hall can still shout tempo to every player; shadow DOM blocks parent descendant selectors on purpose.
SLDS does not automatically make custom SVG charts accessible.
Mobile is not only 'narrow CSS'; some lightning/navigation and toast modules have container rules.

teach_back_prompt: Explain why you would pick a base component over custom HTML, how shadow CSS scoping works, and one mobile constraint, without using a catalog metaphor.

review_schedule.prompt: Name SLDS, accessibility, responsive, and mobile in one sentence each.
Can a parent CSS file style a child's inner h1? Why?
When do you use :host versus a parent c-child selector?
List three accessibility checks you would run on a custom combobox.
Two-minute interview: base component vs blueprint vs custom CSS, plus mobile.

claims.claim: Prefer Lightning base components for built-in SLDS styling and accessibility; otherwise use an SLDS blueprint. Follow WCAG.
Shadow DOM scopes component CSS. A parent cannot style a child's internal elements; it can style the child as a single host. Use :host in the child's stylesheet.
ID selectors are not supported as authored because IDs are transformed into globally unique values at runtime. Prefer classes and styling hooks.

changed_in_release: CSS scope token format changed in past releases (noted in the CSS topic's video callout). Reverify styling hook names against current SLDS for Summer '26.
unresolved_uncertainty: Exact SLDS styling hook names for a given token are not frozen in this pack; look up the current SLDS hooks reference.
Needs verification: Salesforce mobile offline LWC limits for a given feature.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: I start with a base component for SLDS and accessibility. If I must custom-build, I follow an SLDS blueprint, scope CSS in the component, style the host with :host, and use styling hooks. I test keyboard and a phone width, not only a desktop screenshot.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: Shadow DOM means my parent's h1 rule will not restyle a child's heading. I do not fight that with !important from the parent. I handle focus for custom widgets. Hover-only actions fail on mobile. Datatable density is a performance topic too, but overflow is an SLDS/responsive problem first.

terminology.plain: Salesforce Lightning Design System: the visual and interaction language of Lightning.
terminology.precise: Use base components or official blueprints rather than inventing controls. Pair with styling hooks so org themes still apply.
terminology.example: lightning-button instead of a raw <button> with custom hex.
terminology.non_example: A one-off CSS button that copies Slack's colors.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Aura design tokens from older Aura CSS.
terminology.boundary: Token names live in SLDS docs; this lesson is the LWC consumption rules.

terminology.plain: Building so people can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact, including with assistive tech.
terminology.precise: WCAG-oriented: names, roles, keyboard, focus management. Base components include much of this; custom widgets must add it.
terminology.example: Visible label plus keyboard support on a custom LAB_ filter popover.
terminology.non_example: Color-only error (red border, no text) on an input.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Sharing/FLS: who can see data, not who can operate the control.
terminology.boundary: Full legal audit is outside this lesson.

terminology.plain: Layout that reflows when the viewport shrinks or density changes.
terminology.precise: SLDS grid and size classes; hide or stack columns; do not assume desktop record-page width.
terminology.example: Two-column field grid becoming one column on a narrow pane.
terminology.non_example: Fixed 1400px wrapper with a horizontal scrollbar as the 'mobile solution.'
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Salesforce mobile app container limits (modules, navigation).

terminology.plain: Designing the same LWC for phones and the Salesforce mobile app, not only a wide monitor.
terminology.precise: Accessible mobile guidelines, tap targets, no hover-only, test in the mobile container. Some desktop modules are unsupported in other containers (LWC-008).
terminology.example: An action that is a button, not a hover pencil, on a LAB_ list row.
terminology.non_example: A separate Visualforce page 'because mobile' when LWC can reflow.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Responsive CSS only, without container testing.
terminology.boundary: Offline mobile is a neighboring product area; do not invent sync rules here.

terminology.plain: Styles in the component file apply inside that component's shadow tree.
terminology.precise: Prevents leaks and incoming overrides. Parent may style the child host as one element. Child uses :host for its own host. Do not style the same component from both parent and child as a habit.
terminology.example: parent.css cannot change c-child h1 font-size.
terminology.non_example: Global static resource CSS intended to restyle every nested span.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: LWS distortions (LWC-010), which are security, not CSS scoping.
terminology.boundary: Native versus synthetic shadow history is noted; do not invent token strings.

terminology.plain: CSS custom properties SLDS exposes so you theme without hard-coded hex.
terminology.precise: The CSS topic tells you to use global styling hooks for values instead of static font sizes and colors in examples.
terminology.example: background: var(--slds-g-color-palette-neutral-100, #fff); — exact token Needs verification in current SLDS.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Aura tokens in an .css Aura bundle.
terminology.boundary: Look up current hook names; do not memorize an unofficial list here.

when_to_use: When building or reviewing an LWC's SLDS look, accessibility, responsive behavior, or mobile considerations before a UI design review.
When a parent stylesheet fails to restyle a nested heading and you need the shadow DOM rule, not a Salesforce bug report.
When a custom widget has no base component: implement an SLDS blueprint plus WCAG-oriented names and focus.
When a desktop-only hover action will be used in the Salesforce mobile app or a narrow console pane.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this SLDS-and-accessibility lesson as a substitute for Lightning Web Security or CSP (LWC-010) or datatable row limits (LWC-011).
Do not fight shadow DOM by injecting global CSS to restyle child internals, or hard-code hex that ignores styling hooks.
Do not claim a screenshot on a wide monitor proves responsive behavior or mobile considerations.
Do not skip base components in favor of custom HTML just to 'match a Figma pixel' when lightning-* already meets the need.
configuration_or_code_location: component.css next to component.js/html; optional stylesheets static property.
Template: lightning-* base components, SLDS classes such as slds-grid.
js-meta.xml: lightning__AppPage / RecordPage / Salesforce mobile targets as required.
Focus: this.template.querySelector and documented focus handling—not document.querySelector across shadows.

worked_example.scenario: A LAB_ work-queue LWC shows Cases. Design wants a custom status pill, a hover-only edit pencil, and parent CSS to make every nested h1 xx-large. It must work in a utility bar and Salesforce mobile.

decisions.decision: Use lightning-badge or an SLDS badge blueprint, not a div with hex.
decisions.because: Base/blueprint path from the accessibility topic.

decisions.decision: Replace hover pencil with an explicit lightning-button-icon.
decisions.rejected: CSS :hover as the only edit affordance

decisions.decision: Put heading size in the child's CSS via :host or a class, not parent h1.

configuration_or_code: Child uses lightning-button-icon with alternative text.
parent.css may set a border on c-lab-queue-item as a single element.
Grid classes stack the filter row on small widths.
worked_example.output: Keyboard-reachable edit, theme-friendly color, no parent-piercing heading rule.
verification: Tab reaches the edit control on desktop and the button is tappable on a phone emulator.
Child heading size unchanged by parent h1 rule.
Contrast still holds in a dark-themed sandbox if hooks are used—Needs verification per org theme.
worked_example.self_explanation: I treated SLDS and accessibility as product requirements, not polish, and I respected shadow CSS boundaries.

hands_on_lab.environment: Scratch org or Developer sandbox; LAB_ LWC only.
starting_state_checks: You can open the component on a record page and resize the browser.
steps: Create labThemeCard parent and labThemeChild with an inner h1. Set h1 { font-size: 2rem } only in the parent CSS and observe the child heading does not change.
Add :host { display: block; border: 1px solid; } in the child CSS and confirm the host is styled from inside.
Replace a hover-only span with lightning-button-icon that has alternative text; tab to it.
Add SLDS grid classes so two columns stack when the container is narrow; screenshot desktop versus ~400px.
guided_completion: If the child's h1 grew from the parent rule, you are not in shadow-scoped CSS as documented.
If the only edit control is :hover, the lab is incomplete.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Swap a hard-coded color for a documented SLDS styling hook and reload under Lightning's default theme.
evidence: Two screenshots: parent h1 rule does not restyle child text; button is keyboard reachable.
Note that ID selectors were not used.
hands_on_lab.limitations: Does not complete a WCAG certification or Salesforce mobile offline test.

decision_table.signal: Need a button, input, or datatable that already exists as lightning-*.
decision_table.choose: Lightning base component for SLDS styling and built-in accessibility.
decision_table.not: A raw HTML control with custom hex and no name or keyboard support.
decision_table.why: The accessibility topic tells you to prefer base components.

decision_table.signal: No base component, but SLDS has a blueprint for the pattern.
decision_table.choose: Implement the SLDS blueprint plus accessibility attributes and focus.
decision_table.not: Invent a new interaction that designers have not tested.
decision_table.why: Blueprints are the documented fallback when base components do not fit.

decision_table.signal: Parent must visually frame a child card.
decision_table.choose: Style the child host as one element from the parent, or :host inside the child.
decision_table.not: Parent descendant selectors aimed at the child's inner h1 or spans.
decision_table.why: Shadow DOM CSS does not pierce into the child's internals.

decision_table.signal: The only edit control appears on mouse hover.
decision_table.choose: A persistent button with a text alternative; verify on a narrow/mobile viewport.
decision_table.not: Hover-only pencils as the accessibility or mobile strategy.
decision_table.why: Keyboard and touch users never see hover; mobile guidelines apply.

limitations: Does not replace a formal accessibility audit.
Does not list every SLDS class or styling hook.
Does not cover LWS or CSP.
Salesforce mobile offline behavior is not specified here.
security_notes: Do not put secrets in visually hidden text that still exists in the DOM.
CSS does not enforce CRUD/FLS; hidden is not authorization.
Avoid injecting unsanitized HTML to 'fix' layout.
common_mistakes: Parent CSS expected to restyle child internals.
Skipping base components for pixel-perfect Figma.

troubleshooting.symptom: Your CSS does not apply to a nested child heading.
check: Are you in the parent stylesheet targeting inner tags?
Move the rule to the child's CSS or style only the host.

troubleshooting.symptom: Keyboard users cannot reach an action.
check: Is the control hover-only or a non-focusable div?
Use a base button or add tabindex/focus handling per the widget type.
Fixed widths, too many datatable columns, missing grid stacking.
Test Salesforce mobile, not only a resized desktop browser.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: Users will pinch-zoom as the design.

production_notes: Include keyboard and narrow-viewport checks in the definition of done.
Theme changes can break hard-coded colors; prefer hooks.
No production deployment is authorized by this lesson.

mcqs.prompt: What does the Component Accessibility topic recommend when a Lightning base component exists?

options.A: Use the base component for built-in SLDS styling and accessibility
options.B: Always write custom HTML for control

mcqs.rationale: Prefer base components; they provide SLDS styling and accessibility.

mcqs.prompt: Can a parent component's CSS restyle an h1 inside a nested child LWC?

options.A: No; shadow DOM scopes the child's internals
options.B: Yes, always, because CSS is global
options.C: Only if the parent uses an ID selector

mcqs.rationale: The CSS topic's parent/child example shows the parent's h1 rule does not reach the child.

distractor_explanations.C: IDs are transformed and not the piercing tool.

mcqs.prompt: How should a child style its own host element?
mcqs.rationale: The CSS topic uses :host to style the host from the child's CSS.

distractor_explanations.C: That does not pierce the child.

mcqs.prompt: Why does the CSS topic warn against ID selectors in LWC stylesheets?

options.A: IDs are transformed into globally unique values at runtime

mcqs.rationale: ID selectors are not supported as authored because of runtime transformation.

distractor_explanations.B: HTML allows ids; LWC CSS is the constraint.
distractor_explanations.D: Jest is unrelated to this CSS rule.

mcqs.prompt: Which guidelines does the accessibility topic tell you to follow?
mcqs.rationale: We recommend that you follow the WCAG Guidelines for accessibility.

distractor_explanations.B: Colors without WCAG miss the point.
distractor_explanations.D: Query design is not this lesson.

mcqs.prompt: No base component matches a pattern, but SLDS has a blueprint. What next?

options.A: Create a component from the SLDS blueprint
options.B: Skip accessibility because it is custom

mcqs.rationale: If you cannot find a base component, consider creating a component from an SLDS blueprint.

distractor_explanations.B: Custom still needs a11y attributes and focus.

mcqs.prompt: A custom list row reveals Edit only on hover. Keyboard and phone users cannot activate it. Fix?

options.A: A visible, focusable button with a text alternative

mcqs.rationale: Accessibility attributes, focus, and mobile all require an explicit control.

distractor_explanations.D: Does not create a keyboard path.

mcqs.prompt: Parent CSS sets a red border on c-lab-child. Inner text color in the child does not change. Is that expected?

options.A: Yes; the parent styles the child as a single element, not internals

mcqs.rationale: A parent can style a child as a single element (for example a border) but cannot reach inside.

mcqs.prompt: Hard-coded hex versus SLDS styling hooks?

options.A: Hooks keep theme and density; hex fights the design system

mcqs.rationale: The CSS topic tells you to use global styling hooks instead of static values in real component code.

distractor_explanations.B: Contrast still matters, but hooks are the theming tool.

mcqs.prompt: Responsive CSS versus Salesforce mobile considerations?

options.A: Responsive is viewport reflow; mobile also includes container, tap, and hover constraints
options.C: Mobile only means a new Apex class

mcqs.rationale: Narrow CSS is necessary but not sufficient for the mobile app and touch.

distractor_explanations.C: Data access is not the definition.

mcqs.prompt: The CSS topic says it is not a good practice to style a component from both parent and child. Why mention that?

options.A: Combined rules are confusing and can yield unexpected results

mcqs.rationale: The parent/child CSS walkthrough warns against styling from both sides as a habit.

distractor_explanations.B: A parent may still style the host as one box.

mcqs.prompt: Besides using accessibility attributes, what else does the accessibility topic list as required work?
mcqs.rationale: To create accessible components: use accessibility attributes; handle focus.

distractor_explanations.D: Canvas text is worse for a11y.

interview_questions.question: How do SLDS, accessibility, responsive behavior, and mobile considerations show up in an LWC review?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Base components first, WCAG-oriented names and focus, layout that reflows, and no hover-only on phones. Shadow CSS stays in the component.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask whether a lightning-* control already exists. If not, I want an SLDS blueprint, not a one-off. I check keyboard and contrast. I resize the page and think about Salesforce mobile. I treat parent CSS that tries to restyle child internals as a defect in understanding, not a platform bug.
interview_questions.example: labQueue: lightning-datatable plus an explicit action column, not hover pencils.
weak_answer_warnings: It looks like Salesforce so it must be accessible

interview_questions.question: Why can't the parent stylesheet change a child's heading size?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Shadow DOM scopes the child's CSS. The parent may style the child as one host element, not its inner h1.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I cite the Guide's c-parent / c-child h1 example. The fix is to style in the child, use :host, or pass a variant via a public property. I do not recommend global static resources as a piercing strategy. I also avoid styling the same component from both parent and child.
interview_questions.example: parent.css h1 { font-size: xx-large } leaves c-child's heading unchanged.
tradeoffs: Host border from parent versus child :host

interview_questions.question: Design hands you a hover-only pencil on a list row. What do you change for accessibility and mobile?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Make a visible, focusable button with a text alternative. Hover is not a keyboard or touch strategy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I explain WCAG-oriented operable UI. I use lightning-button-icon or a row action in lightning-datatable. I test tab order and a narrow viewport. I do not grow the hover zone and call it done. If space is tight, I use an overflow menu that still opens with a tap or keyboard.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ Case queue row: explicit Edit action instead of CSS :hover pencil.
tradeoffs: Datatable row actions versus custom HTML
follow_ups: How do you label the icon?
What about swipe in the mobile app? (Needs verification)
weak_answer_warnings: Mobile users will learn to hover

interview_questions.question: The org theme changes and your LWC looks wrong. What did you probably hard-code?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Hex colors or px that ignored SLDS styling hooks, so the component did not follow the theme.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The CSS topic's examples even tell you not to copy static values into production components. I switch to hooks, retest contrast, and stop matching a screenshot from a different theme. Accessibility still requires contrast; hooks are not a free pass to tiny gray text.
interview_questions.example: Brand-updated org; custom card still navy from a 2022 hex.
tradeoffs: Hook fallbacks versus exact marketing hex
follow_ups: Where do you look up hook names?

interview_questions.question: Your #submit button styles never apply. What CSS rule did you forget?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: ID selectors are transformed at runtime. Use a class (and SLDS) instead.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I replace #submit with a class and lightning-button if possible. I do not fight the transform. I also check whether the rule lived in the parent trying to pierce a child. Those are two different misses interviewers like to combine.
interview_questions.example: labForm.css #save { } does nothing useful; .slds-m-top_small on lightning-button does.
follow_ups: How do you raise specificity without IDs?

interview_questions.question: A custom combobox is mouse-pretty but a screen-reader user cannot operate it. Where do you start?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Ask why it is not lightning-combobox. Then check accessible name, keyboard, and focus. Custom means you own WCAG work.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I try to revert to the base component. If the blueprint is mandatory, I implement roles, labels, arrow-key behavior, and focus return. I do not add aria-label soup on a div and call it done without a keyboard pass. I mention the Guide's 'handle focus' line so the interviewer hears the official phrase.
interview_questions.example: Custom multi-select rebuilt on lightning-dual-listbox instead.
weak_answer_warnings: aria-label on everything without keyboard support

interview_questions.question: When would you not spend a sprint on custom SLDS CSS?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When a base component already meets the need, or when the real issue is data volume (LWC-011) or security (LWC-010), not paint.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate look-and-feel from performance and LWS. A 5,000-row table will not be saved by nicer badges. A missing label is not fixed by a new palette. I use this lesson when the UI is the product risk: keyboard, theme, overflow, mobile container.
interview_questions.example: Rejecting a custom datatable skin when lightning-datatable plus fewer columns is the actual fix.
follow_ups: Who owns SLDS in your org?
How do you review Figma against base components?
weak_answer_warnings: Custom CSS as the default plan

interview_questions.question: Teach shadow CSS with a concert-hall analogy, then break it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Each musician's mute is their shadow tree. The conductor can frame the whole player as one box but cannot twist an internal peg. That is parent versus child CSS.
